prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, which brought time measurement to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the clearest case on the table of an original idea (Katori's magic-wavelength trapping, which removes the light shift while confining atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime) followed by an experimental programme that delivered what the idea promised. Fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 have been reproduced in several independent laboratories over two decades, the interpretation is stable, and the instruments now serve as probes of relativistic redshift at millimetre scales, of fundamental constants and of dark-sector physics. Four of the eight opening ballots put it first and seven of eight rank it, which I treat as a signal worth examining rather than as merit in itself; on examination the attribution is also the cleanest on the shortlist, since two credited names map onto the proposal and the record-setting realisation. The frequency comb was recognised in 2005 and ion control in 2012, but the lattice-clock step is a distinct invention that those prizes did not cover.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision metrology of this kind is partly an engineering race among many strontium, ytterbium and ion-clock groups, so a two-name prize inevitably leaves out real contributors, and some will read it as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 lines. The redefinition of the second has also not yet happened, so the practical payoff is still prospective. I also rely on recollection of priority questions around early Sr lattice work rather than on verified sources, and I would want the committee to test that point.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the clocks first as an advance in what we can measure and how accurately, with a clean Katori-and-Ye allocation, and raises the possibility of bundling them with other precision lines.
responses.response: I agree on the science and the two-name allocation, but I would not enlarge the prize by bundling combs, molecules or ion clocks. Those lines are either already honoured or are distinct, and a mixed citation would blur what is novel here, namely the magic-wavelength lattice. Where I qualify your view is on the Sr groups outside the two names: the committee should be explicit that the citation is for the lattice-clock concept and its record realisation, not for the whole clock race.

responses.point: Lindroth places lattice clocks first and notes that the 2005 and 2012 prizes honoured adjacent precision-spectroscopy and ion-trap work, so timing is right, while observing that the Cirac-Zoller and Hubbard candidates overlap and credit could be partitioned unfairly.
responses.response: I share the timing argument and think the overlap worry is better answered by keeping the lattice-clock prize single rather than pairing it with a cold-atom theory part. Cirac and Zoller are credited in both B023 and B016, and adding either to B004 would exceed three people or force an artificial split. My preference is a clean one-part prize now, with the cold-atom theory case judged on its own as my first alternative.

responses.point: Olsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, proposing MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero as a two-person pair, and values that the result rests on carefully fabricated structures and is robust although the pairing mechanism is debated.
responses.response: I take the point that a flat-band prediction followed by experiment is a striking theory-to-experiment success, and I kept B010 in my own top three. My disagreement is about maturity: the discovery dates from 2018, the superconducting mechanism is unresolved, and credit among Bistritzer, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, the first author Cao and other groups is still contested. The phenomenon is real, but a prize now would be a bet on how the field settles, whereas the clocks need no such bet. Leaving out Bistritzer in a two-person version also troubles me given the 2011 paper.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube first as a new observational window, citing the diffuse flux and source evidence (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, Galactic plane), while acknowledging allocation problems in a large collaboration.
responses.response: I accept that opening a neutrino window is exactly the kind of clue from nature that the prize favours, and I would not dismiss it. I rank it lower because the source associations are at moderate significance and the three-person allocation within a large collaboration is hard to defend with confidence; I cannot establish from the evidence here what the specific roles of Karle and Yoshida were. Your own second choice was the lattice clocks, so I would ask whether source identification will mature soon enough to make the attribution robust, which could argue for returning to IceCube in a later year.

uncertainties: Whether other lattice-clock proposers or realisations (strontium and ytterbium groups outside Katori and Ye) have priority claims that should alter the credited pair.
Whether the committee will see the lattice-clock step as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
Whether to prefer the clocks now or wait for the redefinition of the second, which would strengthen the application argument but is not needed for the scientific case.
My recollection of the history is not independently verified, and I have less expertise in precision atomic metrology than colleagues in atomic physics.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile: my documented co-authors and institutions (Gothenburg, Max Planck institutes, Oxford, Freiburg) do not include any credited candidate on the shortlist, and my work on turbulence, stochastic dynamics and neural networks is not close to optical clocks.
